extracted.intended_audience: researchers, editors, publishers, platform designers, and scholarly-communication stakeholders interested in peer review reform and platform design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and evaluating hybrid, community-led peer review and publishing platforms that combine features from existing social and publishing systems to provide quality control, certification, and incentives. Focuses on technical, social, and governance criteria for interoperable scholarly-review infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Many journals ask authors to release data to reviewers and for reviewers to report whether they reviewed the data themselves; all data should be made publicly available for evaluation and reproduction (Peer Reviewers’ Openness Initiative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making data available helps correct obvious errors and incentivizes authors to check data and analyses before release; strict enforcement would improve data archiving standards. Beware reviewer burden—reviewers may feel unfairly tasked with checking data without reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple or hybrid peer review models
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrid evaluation methods can be used in series or in parallel (e.g., public GitHub issues, web commenting via Hypothesis, then pre-publication signed review), allowing iterative improvement through different review processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequential/non-conflicting review phases (public drafting, community commenting, formal peer review) can enhance impact and quality; include summaries/appendices of reviews and responses where appropriate. Hybrid combinations should be designed to be complementary and interoperable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of Stack Overflow–style collective validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms that surface practical solutions and their trade-offs (Stack Overflow model) are well suited for research-in-practice by collating community knowledge through collective validation, comparison, and innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mechanisms that surface high-quality, practical answers and allow community ranking to guide reuse and evaluation of research outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Reddit-style discussion threads for engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reddit-style threads (general, loose) are effective for public engagement and hosting virtual conferences or parallel discussion forums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider adjusting reputation/karma systems to give more weight to comments (rather than new posts) to reduce incentives for frequent low-quality posting; use these threads to augment more formal review channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control and moderation as core function
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality control is the core function of peer review; community self-organization and governance combined with a core community of moderators can serve as an alternative to closed editorial systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderators should perform gate-keeping and facilitation akin to editors but in a transparent community context; combine community moderation and crowdsourcing to prevent underdeveloped or non-constructive feedback. Consider electing moderators based on expertise, prior engagement, and transparent reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent moderator identity and persistent identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderator identities should be transparent using persistent identifiers such as ORCID to enable accountability and to leverage researcher metadata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ORCID and similar IDs to create public archives of researcher information that can be used to match referees and avoid conflicts of interest; make identity part of governance and reputation systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Version control and managed-public-review workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: Published objects (pre-prints, data, code, other outputs) should be managed through version control (e.g., GitHub-style) with automated but managed invited review, public interaction, collaboration, and transparent refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the process to focus on constant improvement rather than rejection, allow issues and public comments, close threads when community-decided quality is achieved (while remaining public and re-openable), and assign persistent identifiers (CrossRef DOI) and appropriate licenses to stable versions for indexing and potential journal submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification and reputation for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should be exposed and decoupled from journals to provide formal recognition and certification to reviewers based on engagement and community evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant certification at article and individual levels based on continuing engagement; make certifications and metrics appealing to hiring, tenure, promotion, and funders. Provide portable outputs that can be applied to ORCID and external profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer identification and linking to authorship history
rubrics_metrics.description: For effective certification, peer review should generally require full identification (not anonymous/pseudonymous) to connect on-platform reputation and authorship history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communities must decide identity norms, balancing openness/accountability with privacy concerns; identified participation enables quantification and certification of contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community evaluation mechanisms (up-votes, badges, reputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certification can be provided through community evaluation (up-voting/down-voting, achievement badges) combined with an individual's reputation as an author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transparent quantitative schemes similar to Stack Exchange for achievement and reputation; avoid simple star systems due to bias; outputs should be continuously updated and portable (e.g., to ORCID). Combine with moderation and anti-gaming measures (e.g., token systems, blockchain) to reduce manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives to lower threshold of reviewer engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Incentives are needed to motivate wider participation; lowering thresholds of entry and recognizing effort are essential because academic altruism alone is currently insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify engagement and tie records to ORCID; integrate virtual rewards (points, karma) and hierarchical awards/badges (e.g., 'Top reviewer', 'Verified reviewer') that unlock additional engagement abilities. Highly-rated reviews should gain exposure and credit; consider but be cautious about monetization as it may distort incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Badging and object-level community signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Research objects (papers, data, code) and reviews can carry community-granted badges (e.g., 'Community reviewed', 'Community accepted', '500 upvotes') to quantify engagement and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use badges to create dual incentives: authors to solicit engagement and the community to produce useful feedback. Ensure badges are meaningful and resistant to gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing gaming and low-quality engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs must include moderation and technical/organizational safeguards to prevent gaming (e.g., numerous low-quality engagements) of reputation and certification systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine community moderation, transparent identity, filtering thresholds, and possibly blockchain/token mechanisms to reduce manipulation while preserving openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interoperability and standardised communication
rubrics_metrics.description: A hybrid system requires standardised communication between participants and interoperability across communities to enable uptake and integration into the scholarly ecosystem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify sites for stepwise community adoption, develop interoperable standards for metadata/identifiers (DataCite, CrossRef, ORCID), and design systems that can become de facto standards through high-quality implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of instant messaging / real-time collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Instant messaging services (Slack, Gitter) are analogous to real-time continuous peer review useful for project communication but are distant from other review models as standalone peer review modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use IM tools to supplement hybrid platforms and project-level review, not as the sole mechanism for formal peer review and certification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity, bias, and global inclusion considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation engines and peer review reforms have implications for values, norms, privilege, and bias; systems must be designed with awareness of these socio-cultural effects and the position of researchers from peripheral nations or non-native English speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct evidence-based research on peer review, share publishing/peer-review data, and include community engagement, education, and capacity building to understand cultural needs and reduce systemic bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-led governance and the Principle of Maximum Bootstrapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Research communities should set rules of engagement and provide judge/jury/executioner roles for quality control, making peer review an inherently social, community-led activity decoupled from journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build new systems around existing communities of expertise and norms ('maximum bootstrapping'); ensure governance, certification, and incentives evolve with community activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding over-commercialization and unintended consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of converting principled open practices into mandates or commercialized systems that increase costs or distort incentives (e.g., through monetization or perverse credentialing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design platforms and policies to align with academic needs rather than organizational market goals; prioritize open, community-driven incentives and transparency over monetization.
